opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where the large language model setting both inherits a lot of what we learned from the earlier era of algorithmic fairness and privacy work, and also breaks some of it in interesting ways.

If you go back to the kind of work Aaron Roth and I wrote about in *The Ethical Algorithm*, the basic philosophy was: you have some objective, usually accuracy or some loss function, and then you have a social norm you care about, whether that's a particular notion of fairness or differential privacy, and you try to make that norm precise enough that you can actually encode it as a constraint in the optimization. Then you face a tradeoff explicitly. You get a Pareto frontier between, say, error and unfairness, and the science can tell you what that frontier looks like, but it can't tell you where on it you should sit. That's a policy question, a values question.

With large language models, I think that framing is still the right one at a high level, but a couple of things get much harder. The first is just definitional. In a classification problem, like lending or criminal justice risk assessment, you can say, here's the protected group, here's the outcome, here's false positive rate parity, and write it down mathematically. When the output is open-ended text, what does it mean for a model to be fair, or non-toxic, or not to leak private information? Those notions are much more contextual, and a lot of what's done in practice right now, things like reinforcement learning from human feedback or constitutional-style approaches, is in some sense outsourcing the definition to human raters or to natural-language principles rather than to a crisp mathematical specification. That's pragmatic and it's worked surprisingly well, but you lose some of the ability to make guarantees.

The second issue is where in the pipeline you impose the constraint. You can try to do it at pre-training, by curating the data. You can do it during fine-tuning and alignment. Or you can do it after the fact, with output filters and guardrail models. My bias, coming from the algorithmic side, is that the more you can bake into the training objective, the more principled your behavior tends to be, because post-hoc filtering is often brittle; it's a bit like a game of whack-a-mole, and people find jailbreaks. But in practice you probably want defense in depth, all of the above.

And privacy is an interesting case, because there we actually do have a mathematical definition, differential privacy, and you can in principle train models with it, with differentially private stochastic gradient descent and so on. The challenge at the scale of these models is the cost in utility and compute. But I think it's a nice illustration of the general point: when you can define the behavior precisely, you can constrain it with real guarantees, and when you can't, you're relying more on empirical evaluation and testing.

So I'd say the frontier research question is twofold: first, how do we get better, more precise specifications of the behaviors we want, maybe ones that are contextual but still auditable; and second, how do we measure the tradeoffs honestly, so that stakeholders can make informed choices about where to land, rather than having those choices made implicitly by whoever is tuning the model.

r001.rationale: The response names RLHF as a practical approach for specifying behavioral norms, and separately says constraints can be imposed during fine-tuning and alignment. It does not clearly identify RLHF itself as incorporating those constraints during training.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here. So I think the first thing I'd say is that this is really a continuation of a line of work that goes back a decade or more in the algorithmic fairness and privacy community, which is the idea that you take some social norm or behavioral desideratum — fairness, privacy, now things like harmlessness or honesty or not leaking personal information — and you don't bolt it on at the end as a filter, you actually make it part of the optimization problem. You treat it as a constraint, or as a term in the objective, that the model is being trained to satisfy.

With large language models, the interesting and somewhat frustrating thing is that the constraints we care about are much harder to formalize than something like differential privacy. Differential privacy is a crisp mathematical definition — you can prove a training algorithm satisfies it. Something like "don't give dangerous advice" or "be fair across demographic groups in the way you respond" is not that. So what's happened in practice is that we've substituted human judgment for a formal definition. RLHF, constitutional approaches, preference modeling — these are all ways of saying, we can't write down the constraint, so we're going to learn it from examples of what people say is acceptable, and then fold that into training.

I have mixed feelings about that. On the one hand, it clearly works to a meaningful degree, and I'm not sure there's an alternative for the kinds of fuzzy, contextual norms we're talking about. On the other hand, it means you lose the thing I value most as a theorist, which is a guarantee. You get a model that behaves well on the distribution of prompts you trained and tested on, and you have very little to say about what happens off that distribution — which is exactly where adversaries live. Jailbreaking is in some sense the empirical demonstration that a learned constraint is not the same thing as an enforced one.

The other point I'd make — and this comes straight out of the fairness literature — is that constraints have costs, and you should be honest about them. When we add a fairness constraint to a classifier, we can draw a Pareto curve: here's how much accuracy you give up for each increment of fairness. The same tradeoffs exist for language models — helpfulness versus harmlessness, refusals versus false refusals — but they're much less well characterized, and I think the field would benefit from being more quantitative and more transparent about them, rather than treating alignment as a free lunch or as something that's purely a matter of good intentions.

So the short version is: I think it's the right instinct, it's intellectually continuous with things we've been doing for years, but the move from provable constraints to learned preferences is a real loss, and we should be working hard on getting some of that rigor back rather than assuming the empirical approach will carry us all the way.

r001.rationale: The response names RLHF as one way to learn behavioral norms from human judgments and says those norms are folded into training, rather than added as an end-stage filter.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to view this as a constrained learning problem. You want the model to perform well, but you also want its behavior to satisfy certain requirements. And those requirements need to be part of how you train and evaluate the system, rather than something you simply hope will emerge from making the model bigger.

The difficult part is specifying the constraints. With something like privacy, we have mathematical definitions that let us state precisely what a guarantee means. For a language model, a requirement like “don’t produce harmful responses” is much harder to formalize. What counts as harmful depends on context, and people may disagree about where the boundary should be.

So I would distinguish between encouraging a behavior and guaranteeing it. Human feedback can help steer a model toward responses people prefer, but that doesn’t by itself establish that the model will respect a constraint in every setting. The interesting research question is how to turn those behavioral goals into definitions, training procedures, and evaluations that give us meaningful evidence about what the system will actually do.

r001.rationale: The response says human feedback can steer a model during training, but it does not identify reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) as the example.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to view this as a constrained learning problem. You want a model that performs well, but you also want its behavior to satisfy certain requirements—perhaps about privacy, fairness, or what kinds of requests it will respond to. Those requirements should be part of the training objective, rather than something you hope will emerge from predicting the next word accurately.

The hard part is specifying the constraints. Saying “be fair” or “don’t cause harm” is not yet a mathematical definition, and different definitions can lead to different behavior. Human feedback gives us one way to express preferences, but satisfying the people who provide that feedback isn’t the same as establishing that a model will behave appropriately in every setting.

So I’d distinguish between encouraging a behavior during training and providing a guarantee about it. We have tools for doing the former, and in some narrower settings we can do the latter. For the broad range of situations a language model encounters, there’s still a substantial gap. Incorporating constraints into training is an important direction, but it needs to go together with careful evaluation and an explicit understanding of the tradeoffs.

r001.rationale: The response says human feedback can express preferences and that requirements should be part of training, but it does not identify reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) as the example.
